rows: Cats see about a fifth to a tenth as much detail as people do. This view is blurred to match.
Cats have two kinds of colour-sensing cells in their eyes, where people have three. Reds and greens are hard for them to tell apart, so reds look olive or grey to a cat.
A cat’s pupil closes to a narrow vertical slit, a shape common in animals that hunt by ambush. A slit like this smears out-of-focus things up and down, and this view does the same.
A cat takes in about 200 degrees around itself, and a person about 180. A phone camera sees far less than either, so this view bends the picture at its edges to suggest the wider sweep.
Cats can see in light six to eight times dimmer than people need. This view brightens the shadows to show it.
A phone camera can’t measure distance, so this view assumes that things lower in the picture are closer. Tap the screen to move the focus.
This view assumes that a cat sees most sharply straight ahead.

rows: If you are a domestic cat, a chart test gave one gray tabby about 8 cycles per degree and a younger cat about 18, where a human reads about 30. Behavior studies put cats between 3 and 9.

If you are a domestic cat, you have two kinds of cone, one most sensitive near 450 nanometers in the blue and one near 556 in the yellow-green, where a human has three. Reds and oranges lose their color for you.
In bright light your pupil shrinks to an upright slit, as the pupils of your felid ancestors did. Lions and other large cats keep a round one.
Behind your retina, in the upper back of the eye, lies a mirror-like layer of cells called a tapetum cellulosum. The pigment cells over it carry no dark granules.
If you are a domestic cat, your sharpest sight lies in a cone-rich patch called the area centralis. You have no macula like a human's.
If you are a domestic cat, each degree of a quick eye jump adds about 3 milliseconds to its length. Peak eye speed climbs about 13.6 degrees per second for every degree of jump.

Nobody has measured how fast sharpness fades from your area centralis toward the edge of your sight, or how vivid your two-cone colors are beside a human's. Studies report cats six times as sensitive to light as humans in dim light, but the exact lift and the strength of your eye shine remain guesses.
Nobody has measured some parts of how you see, so they are guesses.
Cats have two kinds of colour-sensing cells in their eyes, where people have three. Reds and greens are hard for them to tell apart, so reds look olive or gray to a cat.
A cat takes in about 200 degrees around itself, and a person about 180. A phone camera sees far less than either, so this view bends the picture at its edges to suggest the wider sweep.
Cats can see in light six to eight times dimmer than people need. This view brightens the shadows to show it.
A phone camera can’t measure distance, so this view assumes that things lower in the picture are closer. Tap the screen to move the focus.
This view assumes that a cat sees most sharply straight ahead.
On this trial the colours come from the measured receptor peaks (450, 550 nm). The camera's colours and the display are the app's.
As the light falls, the colours drift toward what the rods take in, which peak near 501 nm. The peak is measured; where the change happens is the app's guess.

A cat sees in dim light partly by pooling light over time. With &draw=exposure, in the dark the picture pools the last few seconds, so still things settle and moving things leave ghosts. The pooling time is the app's.

windowS.note: seconds of pooling in the dark; the pooling time is the app's (atlas 7)
